\section*{Evaluation}

\subsection*{Setup}

Nineteen machines in one region: nine validator--committer services co-located with nine YugabyteDB
nodes, three signature verifiers, one coordinator, one sidecar, and one load generator. Each has 64
cores and \SI{156}{\gibi\byte} of memory; the database nodes hold their data on local NVMe. The load
generator embeds a mock ordering service, cuts and signs blocks itself, and serves them to the sidecar
over the Atomic Broadcast API, so the figures below measure the committer's validation and commit path
with no ordering service in it. Transactions carry two read--write operations over
\SI{32}{\byte} keys, \SI{262}{\byte} serialized, signed with Ed25519, in
\num{10000}-transaction blocks.

A reported point is the highest offered rate that (i)~arrived in full, (ii)~committed within 2\% of
that rate, (iii)~kept 99th-percentile latency at or below one second, and (iv)~ran with a flat
in-flight count and the sidecar's ledger append below 95\% busy, confirmed by a \SI{300}{\second} hold
on a freshly deployed cluster. Conditions~(i) and~(iv) matter as much as the latency bound: a rate can
be committed in full out of a queue that grows for the whole window, which reports the queue's drain
time as latency. Throughput counts transactions \emph{finished}, committed plus rejected, which is
required for the invalid-signature sweep to mean anything. Latency is measured from block submission to
status, so it excludes the wait for a block to fill --- negligible at the knee (\SI{17}{\milli\second})
and dominant at low rates (\SI{1}{\second} at \num{10000} tps).

\subsection*{Committer throughput and tail latency}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/figure9.png}
  \caption{Throughput and 99th-percentile latency against transaction size, invalid-signature share,
  and double-spend share, against the published figures. Hatched bars are the rejected share, so the
  two experiments are compared at matched reject rates.}
  \label{fig:panels}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:panels} recreates the three published committer panels. Throughput falls with
transaction size, from \num{604545} tps at one read--write operation to \num{274364} at four, a
\SI{55}{\percent} drop over the same range where the published figures fall \SI{41}{\percent}. The
mechanism is not the published one: that account is lock contention in the coordinator's dependency
graph, and on this configuration both lock-wait histograms have a count rate of exactly zero. The
graph's cost is instead per key, about \SI{420}{\nano\second} each and flat from one key per
transaction to eight, so a four-operation transaction costs the graph four times a one-operation
transaction.

Invalid signatures are close to free: \num{558364} tps with none, \num{517455}, \num{519455} and
\num{518727} at \SI{10}{\percent}, \SI{20}{\percent} and \SI{30}{\percent}, flat within
\SI{0.4}{\percent} rather than the published \SI{10}{\percent} \emph{gain}. Rejected transactions are
counted as finished, and the measured reject share matches the configured one to within a tenth of a
point at every step.

Double spends are the one panel that does not reproduce. At \SI{0}{\percent} the same shape holds
\num{518000} tps; at \SI{5}{\percent} and above, no offered rate met the conditions at all --- the
cluster delivers roughly \num{20000} tps with tens of seconds of latency while every machine sits below
\SI{10}{\percent} CPU, so it is neither a capacity limit nor a queue. Reducing the state table's tablet
count from 120 to the default recovers \num{41273} tps at \SI{10}{\percent} double spends, a
\num{2}$\times$ improvement, but a test that narrowed the dependency graph's chunk width refuted the
multi-key batching threshold as the reason. The mechanism is unresolved and the honest reading is that
this deployment has a contention cliff the published figures do not.

\subsection*{What latency the committer costs}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/latency-throughput.png}
  \caption{Latency against throughput at two block sizes. The axis is clipped at
  \SI{400}{\milli\second}; points above it are labelled.}
  \label{fig:curve}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:curve} is the operating curve, and it contains the most actionable result here. At
\num{10000}-transaction blocks the median latency has a floor of about \SI{125}{\milli\second} that
does not fall with the rate, because nothing in a block moves until the block is cut. At 500
transactions a block the floor is \SI{40}{\milli\second}, and \num{380100} tps still holds at
\SI{125}{\milli\second} median and \SI{208}{\milli\second} at the 99th percentile --- the same median
the large blocks give at \num{10000} tps, at thirty-eight times the rate. The upper end of the small
block curve is a measurement of the load generator rather than the committer: its block preparation
caps it near 850 blocks a second, and removing that cap is a separate change.

Table~\ref{tab:size} states the sizes being swept and the published numbers they are compared against.
Size is varied through the read--write value, the only part of this transaction that scales; the
serialized envelope is $202 + 2v$ bytes for a value of $v$.

\subsection*{Threats to validity}

Three, stated because they bound every number above. The load generator is the instrument and twice
became the limit --- once on ECDSA signing, resolved by using Ed25519, and once on block preparation,
which is what caps the small-block curve. A knee is resolved to the search's \SI{8}{\percent} step and
is therefore a lower bound, drawn one-sided in Figure~\ref{fig:panels}. And the cluster's own baseline
drifts about \SI{10}{\percent} between days, so only same-day comparisons on a freshly deployed cluster
are used.
